title: How Monte Carlo heuristics aid to identify the physical processes of drug release kinetics
author: Lecca

steps.title: Set up simulation lattice and cylinder
steps.instruction: Create a cubic 3‑D lattice where each site is a unit‑sized cuboid (side = 1). Define a homogeneous cylinder inside the lattice with initial height 2 H and radius R (later height H is kept constant, radius will shrink). Use a leakage‑region thickness of 1 (the cuboid side).

steps.title: Generate random drug particle coordinates
steps.instruction: Use the R function **generate.points** to place n = 200 random points uniformly inside the cylinder (each point represents 1 mg, so 200 mg drug + 200 mg polymer). For each point draw a random angle θ ≤ 2π, a random radial distance r < R, and a random height z < H. Impose a minimum inter‑point distance d (user‑defined) by calling **buffer.r**, which repeatedly: (1) selects a random point, (2) removes all points within distance d, (3) selects the next random point from the remaining set.

steps.title: Define leak and interior site criteria
steps.instruction: Classify lattice sites by their (x,y) coordinates: • Leak site if (R‑1)² ≤ x² + y² ≤ R². • Interior site if x² + y² ≤ (R‑1)² (can host drug molecules). • Outside site if x² + y² > (R‑1)² (forbidden).

steps.title: Choose Monte Carlo time‑step definition
steps.instruction: Select the MCS (Monte Carlo micro‑step) formula appropriate to the mechanism: • Diffusion: MCS_d = 1 / N(t) (Eq 1). • Erosion: MCS_e = (1/λ)·|ln u| with u ∼ U(0,1) and λ the polymer half‑life (use λ = 0.1 for erosion runs). • Hybrid: MCS = A·[N(t)]^ν + B·ξ(Θ) (Eq 7) or the explicit stepwise form (Eq 8) where A(k)=1/k, B(k)=k, λ1 and λ2 are viscosity‑dependent constants.

steps.title: Perform Monte Carlo particle moves
steps.instruction: Iterate the following until all particles are removed: 1) Randomly select one drug molecule. 2) Randomly choose one of its six nearest‑neighbour lattice sites. 3) If the target site is empty, move the molecule; if occupied, reject the move. 4) If the new site is a leak site, remove the molecule from the lattice and count it as released.

steps.title: Update cylinder radius and leak region
steps.instruction: After each successful move (including removals), recalculate the cylinder radius as R(t) = max_i √(x_i² + y_i²) over all remaining particles (Eq 2). Shrink the cylinder radius by one lattice unit whenever particles are removed from the leak region, thereby moving the leak boundary inward.

steps.title: Increment simulation time
steps.instruction: After each molecule move (or removal) increase the simulation clock by the chosen MCS value (diffusion, erosion, or hybrid) as defined in step 4.

steps.title: Record particle count over time
steps.instruction: At each time increment store N(t), the number of drug molecules still inside the cylinder. This yields the release curve N(t) versus arbitrary time units (a.u.).

steps.title: Fit release curve to Weibull model
steps.instruction: Fit the simulated N(t) data to the Weibull equation N(t)=a·exp(‑b·t^c) (Eq 3) using R’s **nls** function with the “port” algorithm. Report the fitted parameters (example from a single run): a = 1744.943 ± 18.981 (t = 591.929, p < 2e‑160), b = 0.292 ± 0.317 (t = 9.375, p = 3.92E‑100), c = 0.756 ± 0.017 (t = 40.23, p < 2e‑160). Residual standard error = 22.75 on 28 df.

steps.title: Simulate erosion mechanism with exponential MCS
steps.instruction: Run 50 independent Monte Carlo simulations using the erosion MCS_e (λ = 0.1). For each run record N(t) and fit a linear model N(t)=a + b·t (Eq 5).

steps.title: Fit erosion data to linear model
steps.instruction: For each erosion simulation obtain linear‑fit parameters a and b, together with R², p‑value of the F‑statistic, and log‑likelihood. Summarise the distribution of these statistics over the 50 runs (as shown in Figs 5‑7).

steps.title: Implement hybrid MCS (Eq 8) simulation
steps.instruction: Program the hybrid step: Δt_{k+1,k}=A(k)·λ1·N(t_{k+1}) + B(k)·(1/λ2)·|ln u| with A(k)=1/k, B(k)=k. Choose λ1 and λ2 according to polymer viscosity (different for HPMC K4, K15M, 100LV). Run 50 simulations for each viscosity using the same geometry (radius = 4 mm, height = 4 mm, 200 mg drug, 200 mg polymer, n = 200 points).

steps.title: Compare simulated curves to experimental data
steps.instruction: Overlay the average Monte Carlo curves (50 runs) with the experimental release data from Siepmann et al. (chlorpheniramine maleate, HPMC K15M) and Sung et al. (adinazolam mesylate, HPMC 4M, K15M, 100LV). Note that for the Siepmann data the Weibull fit (residual SE = 0.006114 on 10 df, algorithm “port”) matches the simulation perfectly. For the Sung data the hybrid MCS (Eq 8) reproduces the early convex (diffusion‑dominated) portion and the later linear/plateau (stochastic swelling) portion better than pure linear or Higuchi (∝√t) models.
